title: Inversion Basics
grammar_goal: A highly advanced structure (Band 8+) that boosts GRA by reversing the standard subject-verb order to add dramatic emphasis, usually in formal Task 2 essays.

core_rule.formula: Negative Adverbial (Not only, Rarely, Never, Seldom, Under no circumstances) + Auxiliary Verb + Subject + Main Verb
core_rule.usage: When a negative or restrictive adverbial is placed at the very beginning of a sentence for emphasis, the subject and the auxiliary verb must be inverted (like making a question).

when_to_use: Task 2 (Emphasis): To heavily emphasize a point in the body paragraphs or conclusion (e.g., 'Not only is pollution harmful, but it is also costly.').
Task 2 (Conditions): 'Should governments fail to act, the consequences will be severe.' (Inversion instead of 'If').
when_not_to_use: Do not use inversion in Speaking Part 1; it sounds incredibly unnatural and overly theatrical in casual conversation.
Do not overdo it. One or two inverted sentences per Task 2 essay is enough to show mastery without sounding forced.

ielts_examples.writing: Not only does excessive screen time damage children's eyesight, but it also severely impairs their social development.
ielts_examples.speaking: Rarely have I seen such a beautiful sunset as the one we witnessed last night.

repair_section.wrong: Not only pollution harms the environment, but it also causes health issues.
repair_section.correct: Not only does pollution harm the environment, but it also causes health issues.
repair_section.better_band_upgrade: Not only does environmental degradation threaten ecosystems, but it also poses severe risks to public health.

repair_section.wrong: Never I have seen such a terrible situation.
repair_section.correct: Never have I seen such a terrible situation.
repair_section.better_band_upgrade: Never before have we witnessed a crisis of this magnitude.

vietnamese_learner_mistakes: Putting 'Not only' at the start but forgetting to invert the subject and auxiliary verb.
Using the main verb instead of an auxiliary verb for inversion (e.g., 'Rarely go I to the cinema' instead of 'Rarely do I go').
Forgetting to return the main verb to its base form when using 'do/does/did' in inversion (e.g., 'Rarely did he went' -> 'Rarely did he go').

mini_sentence_repair_exercise.wrong_sentence: Under no circumstances you should open this door.
mini_sentence_repair_exercise.correct_sentence: Under no circumstances should you open this door.

mini_sentence_repair_exercise.wrong_sentence: Not only he failed the exam, but he also lost his scholarship.
mini_sentence_repair_exercise.correct_sentence: Not only did he fail the exam, but he also lost his scholarship.

image_prompt_fallback: A visual of a reflection in a mirror flipping an image upside down, symbolizing the grammatical inversion of subject and auxiliary verb.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses negative inversion?

options.A: Seldom we see such dedication in young students.
options.B: Seldom do we see such dedication in young students.
options.C: Seldom see we such dedication in young students.
options.D: Seldom we do see such dedication in young students.

quiz.explanation: Option B is correct. When starting with the negative adverb 'Seldom', you must add an auxiliary verb ('do') and invert it with the subject ('we').
